---
title: "Part 2 – The claim and its estimand"
---
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false}
**Slides.** [Open the deck at this part](../../slides/housing-one-day-methods.html#/part-2-the-claim-and-its-estimand){target="_blank"} in its own tab, or follow it on the [slides page](slides.qmd).
:::

Part 2 is the conceptual middle of the day. It reads the paper, sets out what the five Multi100 analysts did with its claim, and argues that analysts who look as though they disagree are often answering different questions. It then gives you two tools for saying which question you are answering, the estimand statement and the causal graph, and uses both on the claim, where the graph turns up something that is easy to miss.

| Work through | What you do | Timing |
|---|---|---|
| Slides, Part 2 | The paper of the original authors (OAs): the question that it asks, the design, the email word for word, what came back for each of the six names, the four outcomes that were coded, and the claim as SCORE selected it, with its two ellipses. | 16 minutes |
| Slides, the five analysts | The five Multi100 analysts placed by their gaps in percentage points, then a table of what each of them did, with five different questions behind two different verdicts. | 6 minutes |
| Slides, the estimands run | Two studies set beside our five: the red-card estimates again as a single row, the four estimands that the twenty-nine teams were in fact pursuing, and the spread that collapses once the estimand is fixed. Then what under-specified research questions mean for the reading of many-analysts studies, and the steps from a theoretical to an empirical estimand that Lundberg and colleagues set out. | 12 minutes |
| Slides, the causal-graph crash course | Confounders, mediators and colliders; the causal stories that can lie behind one correlation; open and closed paths; total against direct effects; selection and feedback. | 14 minutes |
| Slides, the claim | The estimand statement, which everyone writes in chat, holds and sends together; the causal graph of the experiment; why comparing greetings among the replies conditions on a consequence of the name; and what changes when every delivered email is counted. | 14 minutes |
| Slides, the R tutorial | Optional, if the class wants it: R in one slide, reading and inspecting the data, the verbs that work on rows and columns, tables and tests, model formulas, a plot, causal graphs in R, and the error messages that you are most likely to meet. | 10 minutes |
| [Browser lab](../../cases/housing/lab.qmd#task-2-data) Task 2, or your report or working script, with [Causal graphs and conditioning](../../companion/dags.qmd) as the slower companion | Count the emails that bounced, the replies, the replies with a greeting code and the greetings by name, for each name. Write the estimand statement with every bracket filled, saying which emails you count. Then go to the graph cell of the lab, or open `R/dag_starter.R` in the workspace, take the `#` off the arrow from the name to the greeting if you believe it, ask for the adjustment sets and for the paths with `Z = "reply"`, and read which paths open among the replies. Finish with two sentences: what a comparison among the replies conditions on, and what counting every delivered email changes. | 18 minutes |

**By the end of the part** you have the estimand behind the claim written in one sentence, a graph that includes only the arrows you are willing to defend, and two sentences on why the choice of which emails to count changes the question.
